days.learn: Architecture documentation: C4 and decision records
days.title: C4 diagram for the API side and ADRs for its biggest decisions
days.doneWhen: `docs/architecture.md` shows a C4 level 1 and level 2 diagram in Mermaid that render on GitHub, and `docs/adr/` holds at least four API ADRs, each with context, decision, alternatives and consequences
days.brief:
### Why this matters
After 20 weeks, JobHunt has more moving parts than most take-home projects: cache, queues, jobs, real-time. A reviewer needs a map before reading code, and an interviewer will ask "why did you choose X?". C4 diagrams give the map at the right zoom level; ADRs record each decision with the alternatives you rejected. Today's React part documents the front end the same way.

### What you'll build
On a new branch `release/v1.0`:
- `docs/architecture.md` with two Mermaid diagrams:
  - level 1, context: the user, JobHunt, email, the company info service
  - level 2, containers: browser SPA, nginx, API (with Hangfire inside), SQL Server, Redis, RabbitMQ, blob storage, SMTP, the trace collector
- Arrows labelled with protocol and purpose ("HTTPS JSON", "WebSocket push", "AMQP events")
- `docs/adr/0001-...md` onward for the API side, for example:
  - refresh tokens hashed in an httpOnly cookie, access token in memory (week 8)
  - rowversion optimistic concurrency with 409 (week 10)
  - Hangfire instead of hosted services (week 14)
  - outbox plus RabbitMQ instead of publishing in the request (week 17)
- A template in `docs/adr/README.md`

### Step by step
1. List the ten biggest API decisions; circle four.
2. Draw level 1 on paper: JobHunt as one box, everything else around it.
3. Draw level 2: every container you deploy or depend on, and how they talk.
4. Write both in Mermaid and check they render in a GitHub preview.
5. Write each ADR in under a page: context, decision, alternatives, consequences (good and bad), status.
6. Add the obvious challenge to each ADR and your answer.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  user([Job seeker]) -->|HTTPS| web[SPA via nginx]
  web -->|/api JSON, /hubs WebSocket| api[JobHunt API]
  %% TODO: SQL Server, Redis, RabbitMQ, blob, SMTP
```

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Both diagrams render on GitHub
- [ ] Every arrow is labelled
- [ ] Each ADR names rejected alternatives
- [ ] Consequences include a downside

### Hints
- Levels 1 and 2 are enough for most portfolio projects.
- ADRs are immutable: a changed mind is a new ADR that supersedes the old one.

### Common mistakes
- "Because the course said so" as context. What problem did it solve for JobHunt?

### Check your understanding
- What does each C4 level show, and for whom?
- What makes an ADR useful years later?
- Which API decision would you change today?

days.title: Front end architecture notes: routing, state, data fetching, auth
days.doneWhen: `docs/frontend.md` explains, in under two pages, how routing (data mode, loaders, lazy routes), server state (TanStack Query, keys, invalidation, push updates), client state, forms and auth (token in memory, shared refresh, cross-tab logout) work, with one diagram of the auth flow
days.brief:
### Why this matters
Front-end architecture is often undocumented, so every new developer rediscovers where data lives and why. A short document answering "where does state live, how does data arrive, how does auth work" saves hours and shows you made choices on purpose. It also prepares the answers to the most common React interview questions. Today's .NET part maps the back end; this maps the front end.

### What you'll build
- `docs/frontend.md` with sections:
  - folder structure: `features/`, `lib/`, `hooks/`, `test/`
  - routing: `createBrowserRouter`, loaders with `ensureQueryData`, error elements per route, lazy routes
  - server state: TanStack Query as the only cache, the key factories, `staleTime` choices, optimistic updates, SignalR events patching the cache
  - client state: what stays in components, what lives in context (auth, realtime), what lives in the URL (filters)
  - forms: React Hook Form + Zod, server field errors mapped onto inputs
  - auth: token in memory, shared `refreshAccessToken()`, retry once, BroadcastChannel logout, hub token factory
- A Mermaid sequence diagram for page load and refresh
- A short ADR for the front end's biggest decision (for example: no global state library)

### Step by step
1. Open your router file and write the route tree as a short list.
2. List every query key factory and one line on its `staleTime`.
3. Write where each kind of state lives, with one example each.
4. Draw the auth sequence: page load, refresh, `me`, a 401, a shared refresh, retry.
5. Write the ADR.
6. Ask: could a new developer add a page by reading this? Fix what is missing.

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Every section has a JobHunt example
- [ ] The auth diagram covers the concurrent 401 case
- [ ] Fits in two pages
- [ ] One front-end ADR exists

### Hints
- "Server state vs client state" is the frame most interviewers use; use it too.
- Link to the code rather than copying it.

### Common mistakes
- Describing libraries instead of your decisions.
- A document so long nobody reads it.

### Check your understanding
- Where does each kind of state live in JobHunt, and why?
- Why no global state library?
- How do pushed events and queries stay consistent?

days.learn: Latency budgets and load testing basics
days.title: Measure p95 latency for the main endpoints and fix the worst one
days.doneWhen: `PERFORMANCE.md` records p95 latency for list, detail, stats and status change under a small concurrent load against the production build, each next to a written budget, and the worst endpoint is fixed with before and after numbers

learnLinks.label: Microsoft Learn: ASP.NET Core built-in metrics
Microsoft Learn: ASP.NET Core best practices

days.brief:
### Why this matters
"Is it fast?" needs a number and a target. Averages hide the slow requests users remember; the 95th percentile shows them. A latency budget written before measuring keeps you honest, and a small load test finds problems one request never shows: lock contention, connection pool limits, cache stampedes. Today's React part does the same with Lighthouse.

### What you'll build
- Budgets in `PERFORMANCE.md`: p95 under 200 ms for list and detail, under 100 ms for cached stats, under 300 ms for a status change
- The demo seeder (week 19) plus extra rows so the database is realistic
- A small load: a few concurrent users for a minute, with a tool of your choice or a short script firing concurrent requests
- p95 read from the built-in `http.server.request.duration` metric (week 13's `dotnet-counters` works) or from your traces (week 16)
- The worst endpoint fixed and measured again the same way

### Step by step
1. Write the budgets first, so you cannot move the goalposts.
2. Run the compose stack (week 20) in Release, not the debugger.
3. Run the load and collect p95 per endpoint.
4. Open a trace of the slowest endpoint and find the slowest span.
5. Fix it with week 12 habits: an index, a projection, a cache, less work.
6. Measure again and record both numbers.

```md
| Endpoint            | Budget p95 | Before | After |
| ------------------- | ---------- | ------ | ----- |
| GET /api/applications | 200 ms   |        |       |
```

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Budgets written before measuring
- [ ] p95, not averages
- [ ] One fix with before and after
- [ ] Measured on the production build

### Hints
- Warm up before measuring; the first requests pay for JIT and connection pools.
- Rate limits (week 13) can throttle your own load test; raise them for the run.

### Common mistakes
- Measuring in Debug with the debugger attached.
- Changing two things between runs.

### Check your understanding
- Why p95 instead of the average?
- What can a load test find that one request cannot?
- What was the worst endpoint and why?

days.title: Lighthouse pass on the main pages and fix the two worst findings
days.doneWhen: Lighthouse (mobile, incognito, production build) scores for the applications list and dashboard are recorded before and after in `PERFORMANCE.md` next to written budgets, and the two worst findings are fixed with measured gains
days.brief:
### Why this matters
A performance budget turns "fast enough" into a rule: LCP under 2.5 s, INP under 200 ms, CLS under 0.1 on a mid-range phone. Lighthouse measures the page in a controlled lab run and explains what costs the most. Week 16 gave you field numbers from real browsers; this gives a repeatable lab check to fix against. Today's .NET part does the same for API latency.

### What you'll build
- Budgets in `PERFORMANCE.md`: LCP, INP (or Total Blocking Time in the lab), CLS, and a JavaScript size budget for the main chunk
- Lighthouse runs in Chrome DevTools, mobile profile, incognito, against the nginx-served production build (week 20), three runs per page, median taken
- The two biggest opportunities from the diagnostics, fixed
- Typical candidates: an oversized chunk (week 12 splitting), render-blocking fonts, images without dimensions, a missing cache header in nginx, a layout shift from a late-loading widget

### Step by step
1. Write the budgets first.
2. Run Lighthouse three times per page; record the median.
3. Read the diagnostics, not just the score, and pick the two biggest opportunities.
4. Fix one at a time; rebuild the image each time.
5. Run again the same way and record the gain.
6. Compare with week 16's real-user numbers and write one sentence on any difference.

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Budgets written before measuring
- [ ] Medians of three runs, production build only
- [ ] Two fixes with before and after numbers
- [ ] The main chunk meets its size budget

### Hints
- Extensions skew results; that is why you use incognito.
- Lab and field numbers differ; mention both in interviews.

### Common mistakes
- Running Lighthouse against the Vite dev server.
- Chasing a score of 100 instead of the budget.

### Stretch (optional)
- Add a Lighthouse run to CI that warns when a budget is exceeded.

### Check your understanding
- What do LCP, INP and CLS each measure?
- Why run three times and take the median?
- What did your two fixes gain?

days.learn: Code review checklist for the API
days.title: Self review of the API with a checklist; fix the top issues
days.doneWhen: `docs/code-review.md` holds an API checklist of at least 12 items, the API builds in Release with analyzers on and zero warnings, `dotnet format --verify-no-changes` passes, and the top five findings are fixed in small commits with all tests green after each

learnLinks.label: GitHub Docs: About pull request reviews

days.brief:
### Why this matters
Code written in week 3 was written before you knew most of your current patterns. A checklist turns "review" from a vague read into a repeatable scan, and analyzers catch whole classes of issues for free. Fixing the top findings in small, tested commits is how you clean up without breaking things. Today's React part runs the same review on the web app.

### What you'll build
- An API section in `docs/code-review.md`, grouped by correctness, security, data access, async, errors and tests
- Example items: every query gets the `CancellationToken`; reads use `AsNoTracking` and project; no `.Result` or `.Wait()`; no magic strings for roles, policies, tags or cache keys; every id endpoint has an ownership test; every write publishes after the commit; validation rejects, never clamps
- `AnalysisLevel` set to a recommended level and warnings as errors in Release
- A ranked findings list; the top five fixed; the rest as labelled issues

### Step by step
1. Write the checklist from your own mistakes over the course.
2. Turn on the analyzers; fix or justify every warning with a comment.
3. Review the oldest code first (weeks 3 to 7).
4. Search for `TODO`, `!` null-forgiving operators, `catch (Exception)` and commented-out code.
5. Rank findings: bugs and security first, then consistency, then style.
6. Fix the top five, one small commit each, running tests every time.

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] At least 12 checklist items
- [ ] Zero analyzer warnings in Release
- [ ] Five fixes, each in its own commit
- [ ] Remaining findings are tracked as issues

### Hints
- Refactor in two steps: structure first with no behaviour change, then behaviour.
- If a refactor has no test protecting it, write the test first.

### Common mistakes
- One giant cleanup commit nobody can review.
- Suppressing warnings without a reason.

### Check your understanding
- What is on your checklist that an analyzer cannot check?
- How do you refactor safely?
- Which finding surprised you most?

days.learn: Code review checklist for the web app
days.title: Self review of the web app with a checklist; fix the top issues
days.doneWhen: `docs/code-review.md` also holds a web checklist of at least 12 items, ESLint and `tsc --noEmit` report zero warnings, and the top five web findings are fixed in small commits with all tests green after each

learnLinks.label: react.dev: You might not need an Effect

days.brief:
### Why this matters
React code drifts in predictable ways: effects that should be derived values, state copied from props, query keys typed by hand, `any` sneaking in at the edges. A checklist built from your own course mistakes catches them quickly, and fixing them shows you can improve code, not just write it. Today's .NET part reviews the API with the same discipline.

### What you'll build
- A web section in `docs/code-review.md`, grouped by state, effects, data fetching, types, accessibility and tests
- Example items: no state that could be derived; effects only for external systems, each with cleanup; query keys only from the factories; every mutation invalidates or updates the right keys; no `any` or unchecked casts; no `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` outside `SafeMarkdown`; every form field labelled; tests query by role
- ESLint with zero warnings, `tsc --noEmit` clean, unused exports and dependencies removed
- A ranked findings list; the top five fixed; the rest as labelled issues

### Step by step
1. Read "You might not need an Effect" and list every effect in the app.
2. Write the checklist; add your own recurring mistakes.
3. Search for `any`, `as `, `console.log`, `useEffect` and `eslint-disable`.
4. Review the oldest components first (weeks 3 to 7).
5. Rank, then fix the top five, one small commit each.
6. Run lint, types, tests and E2E after each commit.

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] At least 12 checklist items
- [ ] Zero lint and type warnings
- [ ] Five fixes, each in its own commit
- [ ] Every remaining effect has a reason

### Hints
- An effect that sets state from other state is usually a calculation during render.
- `satisfies` checks a value against a type without widening it; useful for config objects.

### Common mistakes
- Replacing effects with memoisation everywhere "for performance".
- Fixing style before bugs.

### Check your understanding
- When is an effect the right tool?
- What did removing `any` reveal?
- Which finding would an interviewer care about most?

days.title: README: problem, features, stack, how to run, how to test
days.doneWhen: The root `README.md` states the problem, features grouped by user value, the stack, how to run with `docker compose up` and how to test, and you (or a friend) went from a fresh clone in a new folder to a running app using only the README
days.brief:
### Why this matters
Recruiters and hiring managers spend about a minute on a repository, and they start with the README. It must say what the app does, why it is interesting and how to run it, fast. Run instructions that work from a fresh clone prove the project is real, not a pile of code that only runs on your laptop. Today's React part adds the screenshots and the live link.

### What you'll build
- A rewritten root `README.md`:
  - a one-sentence pitch and the problem it solves
  - a features list grouped by user value ("see every application move live across devices"), not by technology
  - a stack section: .NET 10 minimal APIs, EF Core and SQL Server, Redis, RabbitMQ, Hangfire, SignalR, React 19, TypeScript, TanStack Query, React Router, Playwright, Docker, GitHub Actions, Azure
  - "Run it locally": prerequisites, copy `.env.example` to `.env`, `docker compose up`, the URL, the demo login (week 19 seeder)
  - "Tests": the root command and E2E, with what each layer covers (link `TESTING.md`)
  - links to `docs/architecture.md`, the ADRs, `docs/frontend.md`, `SECURITY.md` and `PERFORMANCE.md`
- Placeholders for the React part's screenshots and live link

### Step by step
1. Read two READMEs you admire; note what you read first.
2. Write the pitch: who it is for and what it does, in one sentence.
3. Write features as user outcomes, five to eight lines.
4. Write the run instructions, then follow them in a new folder with a fresh clone. Fix every step you had to guess.
5. Keep it scannable.
6. Add "What I would do next", linking Wednesday's open issues.

```md
# JobHunt
Track every job application from first contact to offer, live across all your devices.
<!-- TODO: live link, badge, screenshot, features, stack, run, tests, docs -->
```

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A stranger can run it from the README alone
- [ ] Features describe user value
- [ ] Test commands are listed with what they cover
- [ ] Every deeper document is linked

### Hints
- Relative links between docs work on GitHub and in forks.
- A demo login saves reviewers a sign-up.

### Common mistakes
- A wall of text before the first screenshot or command.
- Run steps relying on something only your machine has.

### Check your understanding
- What should a reader learn in the first ten seconds?
- How did you prove the instructions work?
- What did you leave out, and where does it live?

days.learn: Screenshots and a live demo link
days.title: Screenshots and a live link in the README
days.doneWhen: The README shows the live link and CI badge at the top, three to five screenshots with real demo data and meaningful alt text (board, live update across two tabs, dashboard, mobile view), stored in `docs/images` at a sensible size
days.brief:
### Why this matters
Most people will look at JobHunt, not run it. A live link and a few good screenshots show in seconds what took 21 weeks to build. Screenshots with realistic data look like a product; "test test 123" looks like homework. Alt text matters too: a README is a web page, and the people reviewing it include screen reader users. This completes the README from today's .NET part.

### What you'll build
- The live link from week 20 and the CI badge at the top of the README
- Screenshots from the live app with the week 19 demo data:
  - the board with cards in every column
  - two tabs side by side after a live update (week 15)
  - the dashboard with charts (week 12)
  - the app at mobile width (week 19)
- Alt text that says what the image shows and why it matters, not "screenshot"
- Images compressed and sized so the README loads fast
- Optional: a short GIF of a drag and live update, under a few MB

### Step by step
1. Seed the demo data in the live or local production stack.
2. Hide bookmarks, extensions and notifications; use a clean browser profile.
3. Capture each screen at a consistent size and zoom.
4. Compress the images and store them in `docs/images`.
5. Write alt text for each, one sentence.
6. Put the most impressive image first, then check the README on GitHub on a phone.

```md
![Kanban board with applications in Applied, Interviewing, Offer and Rejected](docs/images/board.png)
```

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The live link works for a logged-out visitor
- [ ] Every image has meaningful alt text
- [ ] Data looks realistic
- [ ] The README loads quickly on a phone

### Hints
- The demo login in the README lets visitors try the live app without registering.
- Keep the live app's demo data reset regularly if strangers can edit it.

### Common mistakes
- Screenshots with personal email addresses or real job data.
- Huge uncompressed images.

### Check your understanding
- What makes alt text useful?
- Which image goes first, and why?
- How do you keep a public demo tidy?

days.learn: Telling the backend story in interviews
days.title: Interview story sheet: trade-offs, failures, what you would change (API)
days.doneWhen: `docs/story-sheet.md` fits on one page with four backend stories (trade-off, failure, measured fix, what you would change) in situation, task, action, result form plus a next-steps list, each story practised aloud in under two minutes, ready for Release v1.0
days.brief:
### Why this matters
Interviewers do not want a feature list; they want to hear how you think when things are hard. A story about a race condition you found, a trade-off you made or a failure you fixed is worth more than any technology on your CV. Writing them down and practising aloud turns 21 weeks of work into answers you can give under pressure. This is the backend half of Release v1.0; today's React part records the demo.

### What you'll build
- `docs/story-sheet.md`, one page, stories in situation, task, action, result form:
  - a trade-off: the refresh token race and the shared refresh promise (week 8), or rowversion and 409 (week 10)
  - a design: the dual-write problem and the outbox (week 17)
  - a measured fix with numbers (weeks 12 and 21)
  - a failure: something that broke, how you found it (logs, traces, a test) and what you changed
- "What I would change" in one paragraph
- Next steps, each with one line on why:
  - a purge job that hard-deletes long soft-deleted applications and their files
  - ETag and `If-Match` with 412 as an HTTP-native alternative to the version field
  - `HybridCache` replacing the hand-written cache-aside helper
  - an active sessions list with revoke per device
  - the React Compiler, measured against week 12's profiling

### Step by step
1. Pick the four stories you would most like to be asked about.
2. Write each in five or six lines: problem first, a number or a lesson last.
3. Check each against your ADRs; the "alternatives" are your follow-up answers.
4. Practise each aloud twice with a timer; cut what you stumble over.
5. Write the next steps list.

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] One page, four stories
- [ ] Each ends with a number or a lesson
- [ ] One story is an honest failure
- [ ] Each was told aloud in under two minutes

### Hints
- Interviewers probe edges: "what if RabbitMQ is down?", "what if two tabs refresh at once?". Your ADRs hold the answers.
- "I would do this differently now, because..." shows growth, not weakness.

### Common mistakes
- Stories that list technologies instead of problems.
- Reading from the sheet instead of telling the story.

### Check your understanding
- Which trade-off would you mention first, and why?
- What would you change if you started again?
- How would you scale JobHunt to 100 times the users?

days.learn: Telling the front end story and recording a demo
days.title: 2-minute demo video of the full app
days.doneWhen: A captioned 2-minute demo video of the full app is linked from the README, tag `v1.0.0` is on main with a GitHub release whose notes are grouped by feature, and the release links the video, the live app and the docs

learnLinks.label: W3C WAI: Making audio and video media accessible

days.brief:
### Why this matters
A 2-minute video is the one artefact a busy hiring manager will actually watch. A script keeps it tight; showing the live app (not slides) proves it works. Captions make it watchable on mute and accessible. Tagging the release marks JobHunt as finished work you can point to. This completes Release v1.0, together with today's .NET story sheet.

### What you'll build
- A script, timed: problem (10 s), main journey on the live app (60 s), one technical highlight such as live updates across two tabs or the 409 recovery (30 s), the architecture diagram (20 s)
- A screen recording with clear audio, two browser windows side by side for the live part
- Captions (most recording tools can generate them; correct the technical words)
- The video hosted where anyone can view it and linked from the README
- Tag `v1.0.0` on main and a GitHub release with notes grouped by feature, linking the video, live app, `docs/architecture.md` and the story sheet

### Step by step
1. Write the script word for word and read it with a timer.
2. Prepare demo data, a clean browser profile, and the two windows.
3. Record; watch once; re-record only the worst part.
4. Add and correct captions.
5. Merge the release branch, tag `v1.0.0`, write the release notes.
6. Update the README with the video link and share the repository.

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Two minutes or less
- [ ] Shows the live app, including one technical highlight
- [ ] Captions are accurate
- [ ] Release v1.0 is published and linked

### Hints
- Zoom the browser so text is readable in a small video player.
- Do not aim for perfect: clear and working beats polished.

### Common mistakes
- Spending the first minute on setup and slides.
- Recording with notifications or personal data visible.

### Check your understanding
- What should a viewer remember after two minutes?
- Why show the live app instead of slides?
- What do the release notes tell a future reader?

days.title: Whiteboard the full JobHunt architecture (browser to database, including events, cache and jobs) in 10 minutes
days.brief:
### The drill
Whiteboard the full JobHunt architecture (browser to database, including events, cache and jobs) in 10 minutes, then walk two request flows out loud, in 20 minutes total.

### Rules
- Part 1 (10 minutes): blank whiteboard or paper, no notes, no docs, timer running.
- Part 2 (about 10 minutes): trace two flows on your drawing out loud, as if to an interviewer.
- First attempt with nothing open; then compare with `docs/architecture.md` and `docs/frontend.md` and note what you missed. No AI assistants.

### Must include
- Part 1: browser SPA, nginx, API layers, SQL Server, Redis (cache, output cache store, backplane), RabbitMQ, Hangfire, blob storage, SMTP, the trace collector
- Where auth happens: access token in memory, refresh cookie, hub token in the query string
- Flow 1: dragging a card: optimistic update, PATCH with version, 409 or 422 paths, commit with the outbox row, SignalR push to other tabs, cache updates
- Flow 2: the event after commit: outbox publisher, RabbitMQ, idempotent consumer, activity entry, live feed, weekly digest
- One sentence on scaling out and one on what you would add first

### Self-check
- [ ] Drawing finished within 10 minutes
- [ ] Every arrow labelled
- [ ] Events, cache and jobs covered without prompting
- [ ] Both flows included a failure path
- [ ] You know which parts you missed and where they are documented

### If you got stuck
- C4 diagrams and ADRs: Monday, .NET part. Front-end architecture: Monday, React part.
- Performance numbers: Tuesday, both parts.
- Code review findings: Wednesday, both parts.
- Interview stories: Friday, .NET part; then revisit the weeks behind any story you could not tell.
